answer:
Down group 16 the number of quantum shells increases, and every one of these four trends follows from that.

**i. Atomic radii.** Atomic and ionic radii **increase down the group**, because each successive element adds a quantum shell, so the valence electrons lie further from the nucleus. The values are \(\mathrm{O}\) 66, \(\mathrm{S}\) 104, \(\mathrm{Se}\) 117, \(\mathrm{Te}\) 137 and \(\mathrm{Po}\) 146 pm.

**ii. Ionisation enthalpy.** All members have high ionisation enthalpy, but it **decreases down the group**: \(1314 \rightarrow 1000 \rightarrow 941 \rightarrow 869 \rightarrow 813\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\). As the atom grows the valence electron is further from the nucleus and more screened, so less energy is needed to remove it. Across a period the ionisation enthalpy rises with atomic number, but group 16 sits **lower than group 15** of the same period, because group 15 has the extra-stable half-filled \(ns^2np^3\) configuration whereas group 16 has \(ns^2np^4\).

**iii. Electronegativity.** It **decreases down the group**: \(\mathrm{O}\) 3.50, \(\mathrm{S}\) 2.44, \(\mathrm{Se}\) 2.48, \(\mathrm{Te}\) 2.01, \(\mathrm{Po}\) 1.76. The increasing size and screening weaken the pull the nucleus exerts on a shared electron pair. The fall is steep from oxygen to sulfur and gradual thereafter, selenium sitting a shade above sulfur on the scale used in the chapter's table. Oxygen has the highest electronegativity of any element after fluorine.

**iv. Electron gain enthalpy.** It becomes **less negative down the group** from sulfur onwards, since the incoming electron enters a shell further from the nucleus. Oxygen is the exception: its electron gain enthalpy \(\left(-141\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\right)\) is **less negative than that of sulfur** \(\left(-200\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\right)\), because the \(2p\) orbitals of the small oxygen atom are so compact that the added electron meets strong inter-electronic repulsion.

The sequence is therefore \(\mathrm{S} > \mathrm{Se} > \mathrm{Te} > \mathrm{Po} > \mathrm{O}\) in the magnitude of electron gain enthalpy, while radius rises and both ionisation enthalpy and electronegativity fall steadily from oxygen to polonium.

Oxygen, the first member of group 16, differs from the rest of the group in the following respects.

**i. Atomicity.** Oxygen is **diatomic**, \(\mathrm{O_2}\), while the other members of the group are **polyatomic** — sulfur exists as \(\mathrm{S_8}\) rings and selenium and tellurium as long chains.

**ii. Magnetic property.** Dioxygen is **paramagnetic**, while the other members and their common forms are **diamagnetic**. Its molecular orbital configuration
\(\mathrm{KK}\ \sigma(2s)^2\ \sigma^*(2s)^2\ \sigma(2p_z)^2\ \pi(2p_x)^2\ \pi(2p_y)^2\ \pi^*(2p_x)^1\ \pi^*(2p_y)^1\)
leaves **two unpaired electrons** in the antibonding \(\pi^*\) orbitals, and that is what makes it paramagnetic in spite of its even electron count.

**iii. Oxidation state.** Oxygen shows only \(-2\), \(-1\) and \(+2\), whereas the other elements of the group show \(-2\), \(+2\), \(+4\) and \(+6\). Its common state is \(-2\); it is \(+2\) in \(\mathrm{OF_2}\), because fluorine is more electronegative, and \(-1\) in peroxides such as \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\) and \(\mathrm{Na_2O_2}\). Oxygen cannot reach the higher \(+4\) and \(+6\) states because it has **no vacant \(d\) orbitals** into which its paired electrons could be promoted.

All three anomalies trace to the same three causes: the small atomic size of oxygen, its high electronegativity and the absence of inner \(d\) orbitals.

Oxygen, the first member of group 16, differs from the rest of the group in the following respects.

**i. Atomicity.** Oxygen is **diatomic**, \(\mathrm{O_2}\), while the other members are **polyatomic** — sulfur exists as \(\mathrm{S_8}\) rings, and selenium and tellurium as long chains.

**ii. Oxidation state.** Oxygen shows \(-2\), \(-1\) and \(+2\) only, whereas the other members show \(-2\), \(+2\), \(+4\) and \(+6\). It is \(+2\) in \(\mathrm{OF_2}\) and \(-1\) in peroxides such as \(\mathrm{H_2O_2}\). It cannot reach \(+4\) or \(+6\) because it has **no vacant \(d\) orbitals** to promote its paired electrons into.

**iii. Magnetic property.** Dioxygen is **paramagnetic** while the other members are diamagnetic, because its molecular orbital configuration
\(\mathrm{KK}\ \sigma(2s)^2\ \sigma^*(2s)^2\ \sigma(2p_z)^2\ \pi(2p_x)^2\ \pi(2p_y)^2\ \pi^*(2p_x)^1\ \pi^*(2p_y)^1\)
carries **two unpaired electrons** in the antibonding \(\pi^*\) orbitals.

**iv. Nature of hydrides.** The hydride of oxygen, \(\mathrm{H_2O}\), is a **liquid** at room temperature, while \(\mathrm{H_2S}\), \(\mathrm{H_2Se}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2Te}\) are **gases**. Water boils at 373 K against 213 K for \(\mathrm{H_2S}\), because the small, highly electronegative oxygen atom lets water molecules associate through strong **intermolecular hydrogen bonding**, which the heavier hydrides cannot do.

All four anomalies follow from the same three causes: small atomic size, high electronegativity and the absence of inner \(d\) orbitals.

**Reason.** A group 15 element has the valence configuration \(ns^2np^3\), in which the three \(p\) electrons occupy the three \(p\) orbitals singly. This **half-filled \(p\) sub-shell is extra stable**, so a large amount of energy is needed to disturb it by removing an electron.

A group 16 element of the same period has \(ns^2np^4\). The fourth \(p\) electron has to pair up in an orbital that already holds one electron, and the **inter-electronic repulsion within that pair** makes it easier to remove.

Hence, in the same period, group 16 elements have the **lower first ionisation enthalpy** — for example \(\mathrm{O}\ 1314\) against \(\mathrm{N}\ 1402\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), and \(\mathrm{S}\ 1000\) against \(\mathrm{P}\ 1012\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\).

**Two uses of dioxygen.**
1. In the **manufacture of steel**.
2. In the **oxyacetylene flame** used for welding and cutting metals.

The chapter also lists respiration in animal and aquatic life, oxygen cylinders in hospitals and for high-altitude flying and mountaineering, and the combustion of fuels.

\(\mathrm{H_2O_2} + \mathrm{O_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2}\)

The peroxide loses one of its two oxygen atoms — it is reduced — so this reaction illustrates the **reducing property of ozone**, which it shows towards peroxides. Ozone reduces barium peroxide in the same way:

\(\mathrm{BaO_2} + \mathrm{O_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{BaO} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2}\)

Counting the atoms confirms the first equation: two hydrogen and five oxygen atoms on each side.

Ozone bleaches because it is a powerful **oxidising agent**. It decomposes readily to give **nascent oxygen**, and that nascent oxygen oxidises the coloured matter to a colourless product:

\(\mathrm{O_3} \longrightarrow \mathrm{O_2} + [\mathrm{O}]\)

\(\text{Coloured matter} + [\mathrm{O}] \longrightarrow \text{Colourless matter}\)

Nothing in either step needs water. **Ozone therefore bleaches in the absence of moisture**, and for that reason its bleaching action is called a **dry bleach**.

The contrast with chlorine makes the point. Chlorine bleaches only in the presence of moisture, because it must first react with water to give hypochlorous acid before any nascent oxygen is available:

\(\mathrm{Cl_2} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HCl} + \mathrm{HOCl}\)

\(\mathrm{HOCl} \longrightarrow \mathrm{HCl} + [\mathrm{O}]\)

Ozone needs no such step, so it is the dry bleach and chlorine is not.

**(A)** \(\mathrm{NO}\)

Nitric oxide is the nitrogen species that attacks ozone. It is oxidised by ozone to nitrogen dioxide, and the ozone molecule is destroyed in the process:

\(\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_3(g)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}\)

The nitric oxide emitted from the exhaust systems of supersonic jet aeroplanes therefore brings about depletion of the ozone layer in the upper atmosphere.

Of the remaining three species, \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) is the **product** of that reaction rather than the attacking molecule, and \(\mathrm{NO_3}\) and \(\mathrm{N_2O_5}\) are named nowhere in the chapter's account of ozone depletion, whose only other stated cause is chlorofluorocarbons. Nitric oxide is the answer.

\(2x = 12\), so \(x = +6\) for each sulfur.

In every one of these acids the ionisable hydrogen is attached to oxygen and not to sulfur. What distinguishes them is whether the two sulfurs are joined directly, through a bridging oxygen or through a peroxide linkage, and how many doubly bonded oxygens each sulfur carries.

| Acid | Molecular formula | Structure | Oxidation state of S |
|---|---|---|---|
| a. Dithionic acid | \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_6}\) | \(\mathrm{HO-SO_2-SO_2-OH}\) — a **direct S-S bond**, each sulfur carrying two \(\mathrm{S{=}O}\) bonds and one \(\mathrm{-OH}\) | \(+5\) |
| b. Peroxymonosulphuric acid | \(\mathrm{H_2SO_5}\) | \(\mathrm{HO-O-SO_2-OH}\) — one sulfur bearing two \(\mathrm{S{=}O}\) bonds, one \(\mathrm{-OH}\) and one **peroxide \(\mathrm{-O-O-H}\)** group | \(+6\) |
| c. Pyrosulphuric acid | \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\) | \(\mathrm{HO-SO_2-O-SO_2-OH}\) — two \(\mathrm{-SO_3H}\) units joined through a **bridging oxygen** | \(+6\) |
| d. Dithionous acid | \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_4}\) | \(\mathrm{HO-SO-SO-OH}\) — a **direct S-S bond**, each sulfur carrying only one \(\mathrm{S{=}O}\) bond and one \(\mathrm{-OH}\) | \(+3\) |

Each oxidation state follows from taking \(\mathrm{H}\) as \(+1\) and \(\mathrm{O}\) as \(-2\), except for the two peroxide oxygens of \(\mathrm{H_2SO_5}\), which are \(-1\):

\(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_6}:\ 2 + 2x - 12 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +5\)

\(\mathrm{H_2SO_5}:\ 2 + x + 3(-2) + 2(-1) = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\)

\(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}:\ 2 + 2x - 14 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +6\)

\(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_4}:\ 2 + 2x - 8 = 0 \Rightarrow x = +3\)

Counting the atoms of each written structure returns its molecular formula, so the four structures and formulae agree.

**Preparation of sulphur dioxide from sulphur.** Sulphur burns in air to give sulphur dioxide:

\(\mathrm{S(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{SO_2(g)}\)

One atom of sulphur and two of oxygen appear on each side, so the equation is balanced as written. The gas obtained is colourless, poisonous and has a pungent smell.

**Uses of sulphur** (any two):
1. In the **manufacture of sulphuric acid**, where it is the starting material for the first step of the contact process, \(\mathrm{S} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{SO_2}\).
2. In the **vulcanisation of rubber**, which makes the rubber hard and elastic.
3. In the manufacture of gunpowder, matches and fireworks.
4. As a **fungicide** in agriculture, and in ointments used for skin diseases.

**i. Chloric acid, \(\mathrm{HClO_3}\).**

\(\mathrm{HO-ClO_2}\), that is \(\mathrm{H-O-Cl}\) with the chlorine also carrying **two \(\mathrm{Cl{=}O}\) double bonds**.

The ionisable hydrogen is attached to oxygen and not to chlorine, as in every oxoacid of chlorine. The chlorine has three bonded oxygens and one lone pair, so the arrangement about it is **pyramidal**. Its oxidation state is \(+5\), since \(+1 + x + 3(-2) = 0\) gives \(x = +5\), which places it third in the series \(\mathrm{HOCl}\), \(\mathrm{HClO_2}\), \(\mathrm{HClO_3}\), \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\).

**ii. Peroxydisulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_8}\).**

\(\mathrm{HO-SO_2-O-O-SO_2-OH}\)

Two \(\mathrm{-SO_3H}\) units, each with a tetrahedral sulfur carrying two \(\mathrm{S{=}O}\) bonds and one \(\mathrm{-OH}\), joined to each other through a **peroxide \(\mathrm{-O-O-}\) linkage**. It is that peroxide bridge which distinguishes it from pyrosulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{HO-SO_2-O-SO_2-OH}\), where a single oxygen does the bridging.

Each sulfur is in the \(+6\) state: with the two peroxide oxygens at \(-1\) and the other six at \(-2\), \(2 + 2x - 12 - 2 = 0\) gives \(x = +6\). Counting the atoms of the written structure gives two hydrogen, two sulfur and eight oxygen, which is the stated formula.

**i. Sulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\).**

\(\mathrm{(HO)_2SO_2}\), that is \(\mathrm{HO-SO_2-OH}\): the sulfur carries **two \(\mathrm{S{=}O}\) double bonds and two \(\mathrm{S{-}OH}\) single bonds**, arranged **tetrahedrally** about it. Both ionisable hydrogens are attached to oxygen, which is why the acid is dibasic. The oxidation state of sulfur is \(+6\), from \(2(+1) + x + 4(-2) = 0\).

**ii. Thiosulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_3}\).**

\(\mathrm{(HO)_2S(=O)(=S)}\), that is \(\mathrm{HO-S(=O)(=S)-OH}\): the same tetrahedral skeleton as sulphuric acid with **one of the two doubly bonded oxygens replaced by a sulfur atom**. The prefix *thio-* records exactly that replacement.

Because the two sulfur atoms are not equivalent, their oxidation states differ: the central sulfur is \(+6\) and the terminal sulfido sulfur is \(-2\), which averages to \(+2\) — the value \(2(+1) + 2x + 3(-2) = 0\) returns. Counting the atoms of each structure returns \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_3}\) respectively.

**Peroxymonosulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{H_2SO_5}\)** (Caro's acid).

\(\mathrm{HO-O-SO_2-OH}\)

The single sulfur atom is **tetrahedral** and carries four groups: **two \(\mathrm{S{=}O}\) double bonds**, one ordinary \(\mathrm{S{-}OH}\) group, and one \(\mathrm{S{-}O{-}O{-}H}\) group containing a **peroxide linkage**. It is that \(\mathrm{-O-O-}\) bridge that makes the acid a *peroxy* acid and distinguishes it from sulphuric acid, \(\mathrm{HO-SO_2-OH}\).

The oxidation state of sulfur is \(+6\). Taking the two peroxide oxygens as \(-1\) and the remaining three as \(-2\):

\(2(+1) + x + 3(-2) + 2(-1) = 0\)

\(x = +6\)

Counting the atoms of the written structure gives two hydrogen, one sulfur and five oxygen, which is the stated formula \(\mathrm{H_2SO_5}\).

In the **lead chamber process** sulphur dioxide is oxidised to sulphuric acid inside lead-lined chambers, with oxides of nitrogen acting as the **oxygen carrier**. The steps are as follows.

**Step 1 — production of sulphur dioxide.** Sulphur is burnt in air, or a sulphide ore such as iron pyrites is roasted:

\(\mathrm{S(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{SO_2(g)}\)

\(4\,\mathrm{FeS_2(s)} + 11\,\mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,\mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s)} + 8\,\mathrm{SO_2(g)}\)

**Step 2 — oxidation of nitric oxide.** In the chamber, nitric oxide is oxidised by the air present:

\(2\,\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{NO_2(g)}\)

**Step 3 — oxidation of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) in the chamber.** Nitrogen dioxide oxidises the sulphur dioxide in the presence of steam, and the nitric oxide is regenerated:

\(\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{NO_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} + \mathrm{NO(g)}\)

Because the nitric oxide reappears, steps 2 and 3 repeat over and over, and the nitrogen oxides are not consumed. Adding twice step 3 to step 2 cancels them and gives the **overall change**:

\(2\,\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O(l)} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)}\)

**Step 4 — recovery of the nitrogen oxides.** The gases leaving the chambers still carry nitrogen oxides. In the **Gay-Lussac tower** they are absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid as nitrosylsulphuric acid, the so-called chamber crystals:

\(\mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{NO_2(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{NOHSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

In the **Glover tower** the same compound is decomposed by water and the oxides are returned to the chambers:

\(2\,\mathrm{NOHSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\,\mathrm{H_2SO_4} + \mathrm{NO(g)} + \mathrm{NO_2(g)}\)

The acid drawn from the chambers is dilute, about 62 to 70 per cent, and is concentrated in the Glover tower. Each equation balances: the overall change carries two sulphur, four hydrogen and eight oxygen atoms on each side, and the Gay-Lussac equation two nitrogen, four hydrogen, two sulphur and eleven oxygen on each side.

Fluorine, the first member of group 17, differs from the other halogens because of its **small atomic size, its very high electronegativity, the absence of \(d\) orbitals in its valence shell** and its low \(\mathrm{F{-}F}\) bond dissociation enthalpy. The three properties asked about follow from these.

**a. Hydrogen bonding.** Fluorine is the most electronegative element, so the \(\mathrm{H{-}F}\) bond is strongly polar and the small fluorine atom carries a concentrated negative charge. Hydrogen fluoride molecules therefore associate through **strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding**, and \(\mathrm{HF}\) is a **liquid** (b.p. 293 K) while \(\mathrm{HCl}\), \(\mathrm{HBr}\) and \(\mathrm{HI}\) are **gases** (b.p. 189, 206 and 238 K). The other halogens are too large and too weakly electronegative for their hydrides to hydrogen bond.

**b. Oxidation state.** Fluorine shows **only \(-1\)**, whereas chlorine, bromine and iodine show \(-1\), \(+1\), \(+3\), \(+5\) and \(+7\). Being the most electronegative element, fluorine can never be assigned a positive oxidation state; and having **no \(d\) orbitals in its valence shell**, it cannot unpair and promote its electrons, so it forms only one covalent bond.

**c. Polyhalide ions.** Polyhalide ions such as \(\mathrm{Cl_3^-}\) in \(\mathrm{K^+[Cl_3]^-}\) and \(\mathrm{I_5^-}\) in \(\mathrm{[NH_4]^+[I_5]^-}\) require the central halogen to hold more than the octet, which again needs vacant \(d\) orbitals. **Fluorine has none, so it forms no polyhalide ions.** The same limitation shows up in the interhalogens: fluorine appears in \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\), \(\mathrm{BrF_5}\) and \(\mathrm{IF_7}\) only as the surrounding halogen and **never as the central atom**.

answer:
Fluorine, the first member of group 17, differs in properties from the rest of the group for **four reasons**:

1. its **small atomic size** (atomic radius 64 pm against 99 pm for chlorine);
2. its **highest electronegativity** of all the elements (4.0);
3. the **absence of \(d\) orbitals in its valence shell**, which is only the second shell;
4. its **low \(\mathrm{F{-}F}\) bond dissociation enthalpy**, caused by the strong repulsion between the lone pairs of the two small, closely held fluorine atoms.

These show themselves as the following anomalies.

- Its **ionisation enthalpy, electronegativity and electrode potential are all higher** than the trend of the other halogens would predict.
- Its **ionic and covalent radii, melting point, boiling point and electron gain enthalpy are all lower** than expected. Its electron gain enthalpy \(\left(-333\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\right)\) is less negative than that of chlorine \(\left(-349\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\right)\), because the incoming electron meets strong repulsion in the compact \(2p\) orbitals.
- **Most of its reactions are exothermic**, since the bonds it forms with other elements are short and strong.
- It forms **only one oxoacid**, \(\mathrm{HOF}\), while the other halogens form several.
- **Hydrogen fluoride is a liquid** because of strong hydrogen bonding, while the other hydrogen halides are gases.
- It shows **only the \(-1\) oxidation state**, while the others also show \(+1\), \(+3\), \(+5\) and \(+7\).

The first two members of group 17, the halogen family, are **fluorine** and **chlorine**.

**Fluorine**, \(\mathrm{F}\), \(Z = 9\):

\(1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^5\), that is \(\mathrm{[He]}\,2s^2 2p^5\)

**Chlorine**, \(\mathrm{Cl}\), \(Z = 17\):

\(1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ 3p^5\), that is \(\mathrm{[Ne]}\,3s^2 3p^5\)

Both fit the general valence shell configuration of the group, \(ns^2np^5\): each has **seven electrons in its valence shell**, one short of the stable configuration of the nearest noble gas, which is why a halogen gains or shares one electron and shows the \(-1\) oxidation state. The electron counts check: \(2 + 2 + 5 = 9\) for fluorine and \(2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 5 = 17\) for chlorine.

**a. Two uses of sulphur.**
1. In the **manufacture of sulphuric acid** — sulphur burnt in air gives \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), the first step of the contact process, \(\mathrm{S} + \mathrm{O_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{SO_2}\).
2. In the **vulcanisation of rubber**, which makes it hard and elastic.

Sulphur is also used in gunpowder, matches and fireworks, as a fungicide in agriculture, and in ointments for skin diseases.

**b. Two uses of chlorine.**
1. For the **purification (sterilizing) of drinking water**.
2. For **bleaching** wood pulp in the manufacture of paper and rayon, and for bleaching cotton and textiles.

The chapter also gives the extraction of metals such as gold and platinum; the manufacture of dyes, drugs and organic compounds such as \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\), \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and DDT; and the preparation of poisonous gases such as phosgene and tear gas.

Chlorine reacts with **dry slaked lime**, \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}\), to give **bleaching powder**:

\(2\,\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} + 2\,\mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OCl)_2} + \mathrm{CaCl_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The chlorine **disproportionates**: half of it is reduced to the chloride of \(\mathrm{CaCl_2}\), where its oxidation state is \(-1\), and half is oxidised to the hypochlorite of \(\mathrm{Ca(OCl)_2}\), where it is \(+1\). It is the hypochlorite that gives bleaching powder its bleaching and disinfecting action.

The equation balances: two calcium, four chlorine, four hydrogen and four oxygen atoms appear on each side.

When ammonia is present **in excess**, chlorine oxidises it to nitrogen and the ammonia left over takes up the hydrogen chloride formed, so the products are **ammonium chloride and nitrogen**:

\(8\,\mathrm{NH_3}\ (\text{excess}) + 3\,\mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow 6\,\mathrm{NH_4Cl} + \mathrm{N_2}\)

The equation balances: eight nitrogen, twenty-four hydrogen and six chlorine atoms on each side.

The proportion matters. If the **chlorine** is in excess instead, the product is the explosive nitrogen trichloride:

\(\mathrm{NH_3} + 3\,\mathrm{Cl_2}\ (\text{excess}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{NCl_3} + 3\,\mathrm{HCl}\)

**Chlorine trifluoride, \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\)**, is an interhalogen of the type \(\mathrm{XX'_3}\), in which chlorine is the larger and more electropositive halogen and is therefore the **central atom**.

**Electron count.** Chlorine has seven valence electrons. Three of them form single bonds to the three fluorine atoms, leaving **two lone pairs** on chlorine. The central atom therefore holds

\(3\ \text{bond pairs} + 2\ \text{lone pairs} = 5\ \text{electron pairs}\)

**Hybridisation and geometry.** Five electron pairs require \(sp^3d\) hybridisation, so the electron pairs point to the corners of a **trigonal bipyramid**. The two lone pairs take the two **equatorial** positions, because a lone pair needs more room than a bond pair and the equatorial sites suffer the least repulsion there.

**Shape.** What remains occupied by atoms is one equatorial and two axial fluorines, so the molecule is **bent T-shaped**. The lone pairs push the two axial bonds towards the equatorial one, so the \(\mathrm{F{-}Cl{-}F}\) angle is squeezed from \(90^\circ\) down to about \(89^\circ\).

The oxidation state of the central chlorine is \(+3\), consistent with the two lone pairs the chapter's table records for \(\mathrm{ClF_3}\), \(\mathrm{BrF_3}\) and \(\mathrm{IF_3}\).

**Interhalogen compounds.**

An **interhalogen compound is a neutral compound formed by the combination of atoms of two different halogens**. Although all halogens belong to the same group they differ in electronegativity, and it is that difference which lets one halogen combine with another.

The general formula is \(\mathrm{XX'_n}\), where \(\mathrm{X}\) is the **larger and more electropositive** halogen, which acts as the central atom, and \(\mathrm{X'}\) is the smaller and more electronegative one; the compound is named as the halide of \(\mathrm{X}\). A halogen combines only with a halogen of **lower electronegativity than itself**, which is why fluorine is never the central atom. Four types exist, \(\mathrm{XX'}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_3}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_5}\) and \(\mathrm{XX'_7}\), the value of \(n\) being limited by how much larger \(\mathrm{X}\) is than \(\mathrm{X'}\) — hence \(\mathrm{IF_7}\) exists but \(\mathrm{ClF_7}\) does not.

Examples: \(\mathrm{ClF}\) (chlorine monofluoride), \(\mathrm{BrF_3}\) (bromine trifluoride), \(\mathrm{IF_5}\) and \(\mathrm{IF_7}\).

**Preparation of oxygen.**

**a. From potassium chlorate**, heated with manganese dioxide as catalyst:

\(2\,\mathrm{KClO_3(s)} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{MnO_2}]{\Delta} 2\,\mathrm{KCl(s)} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2(g)}\)

**b. From lead dioxide**, by thermal decomposition of the higher oxide to the lower:

\(2\,\mathrm{PbO_2(s)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\,\mathrm{PbO(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)}\)

Both equations balance as written, the first carrying two potassium, two chlorine and six oxygen atoms on each side and the second two lead and four oxygen.

answer:
**Interhalogen compounds.**

An **interhalogen compound is a neutral compound formed by the combination of atoms of two different halogens**. All halogens belong to the same group but differ in electronegativity, and that difference is what lets them combine with one another.

The general formula is \(\mathrm{XX'_n}\), with \(\mathrm{X}\) the **larger, more electropositive** halogen as central atom and \(\mathrm{X'}\) the smaller, more electronegative one; the compound is named as the halide of \(\mathrm{X}\). Four types exist, \(\mathrm{XX'}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_3}\), \(\mathrm{XX'_5}\) and \(\mathrm{XX'_7}\). Examples are \(\mathrm{ClF}\) (chlorine monofluoride) and \(\mathrm{BrF_3}\) (bromine trifluoride).

**Chlorine with dry slaked lime.**

Chlorine reacts with dry slaked lime, \(\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2}\), to give **bleaching powder**:

\(2\,\mathrm{Ca(OH)_2} + 2\,\mathrm{Cl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Ca(OCl)_2} + \mathrm{CaCl_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}\)

The chlorine disproportionates, half of it going to \(-1\) in the chloride and half to \(+1\) in the hypochlorite; it is the hypochlorite that bleaches. The equation carries two calcium, four chlorine, four hydrogen and four oxygen atoms on each side.

**(i) Acidic strength of the oxoacids of chlorine.**

\(\mathrm{HOCl} < \mathrm{HClO_2} < \mathrm{HClO_3} < \mathrm{HClO_4}\)

The acid strength of a halogen oxoacid **increases with the oxidation state of the halogen**, here \(+1, +3, +5, +7\). Each added oxygen pulls electron density away from the \(\mathrm{O{-}H}\) bond and spreads the negative charge of the anion left behind over more oxygens, so the proton is released more readily. Thus \(\mathrm{HOCl}\) is a weak acid, \(K_a = 3.5 \times 10^{-8}\), while \(\mathrm{HClO_4}\) is very strong, \(K_a \gg 1\).

**(ii) Ionic character of the halides.**

\(\mathrm{MI} < \mathrm{MBr} < \mathrm{MCl} < \mathrm{MF}\)

The ionic character of an \(\mathrm{M{-}X}\) bond **increases with the electronegativity difference** between the metal and the halogen. Electronegativity falls down group 17 — \(\mathrm{F}\ 4.0\), \(\mathrm{Cl}\ 3.2\), \(\mathrm{Br}\ 3.0\), \(\mathrm{I}\ 2.7\) — so for the same metal the difference is greatest with fluorine and least with iodine. The large, easily polarised iodide ion also gives the \(\mathrm{M{-}I}\) bond the most covalent character.

**(iii) Thermal stability of the hydrogen halides.**

\(\mathrm{HI} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HF}\)

Thermal stability follows the **\(\mathrm{H{-}X}\) bond dissociation enthalpy**, which falls down the group as the halogen grows and the bond lengthens: \(\mathrm{HF}\ 574\), \(\mathrm{HCl}\ 432\), \(\mathrm{HBr}\ 363\), \(\mathrm{HI}\ 295\ \mathrm{kJ\ mol^{-1}}\), for bond lengths of 91.7, 127.4, 141.4 and 160.9 pm. The weakest bond breaks first, so \(\mathrm{HI}\) is the least stable and \(\mathrm{HF}\) the most.

Note that acidic strength runs the **opposite** way to thermal stability, \(\mathrm{HF} < \mathrm{HCl} < \mathrm{HBr} < \mathrm{HI}\), and for the same reason: the weaker the \(\mathrm{H{-}X}\) bond, the more easily the proton is given up.

answer:
**a. Sulphur**, \(\mathrm{S}\), \(Z = 16\):

\(1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ 3p^4\), that is \(\mathrm{[Ne]}\,3s^2 3p^4\)

The electrons total \(2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 4 = 16\). The valence shell is \(3s^2 3p^4\), the \(ns^2np^4\) configuration of group 16, so sulphur needs two more electrons to reach the argon configuration.

**b. Krypton**, \(\mathrm{Kr}\), \(Z = 36\):

\(1s^2\ 2s^2\ 2p^6\ 3s^2\ 3p^6\ 3d^{10}\ 4s^2\ 4p^6\), that is \(\mathrm{[Ar]}\,3d^{10} 4s^2 4p^6\)

Filling follows the increasing order of energy \(4s\) before \(3d\) before \(4p\), and the electrons total \(2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 6 + 10 + 2 + 6 = 36\). The valence shell is \(4s^2 4p^6\), the \(ns^2np^6\) configuration of group 18, which is why krypton is a noble gas.

**Two uses of neon.**

1. In **neon discharge lamps and signs**. The light from these signs is visible from long distances and passes through mist and fog, which is why they are used for advertising and for beacons.
2. In **fluorescent tubes**.

The chapter also gives two further uses: a mixture of neon and helium is used in protective electrical devices such as voltage stabilizers and current rectifiers, and neon is used in the production of lasers.
